claims.text: Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Resistance to temper embrittlement is the reason these alloy systems can produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Temperature variation is the intervention used to induce the proposed transition.
The relevant behavior occurs within a narrow temperature window.
Alloy composition and microstructure mediate the response to temperature.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys resist temper embrittlement.
The proposed material will undergo a ductile–brittle–ductile transition without a dramatic loss of ductility.
Conventional alloys exhibit temper embrittlement and serve as the baseline.
There is a temperature range in which temper embrittlement occurs in conventional alloys.

contradictions.description: Resistance to temper embrittlement supports retention of ductility, but it does not explain the proposed intermediate brittle state. The stated mechanism therefore conflicts with or fails to generate the ductile–brittle–ductile outcome.
A ductile-to-brittle transition ordinarily entails a substantial reduction in ductility, whereas the outcome simultaneously specifies that the transition occurs without a dramatic loss of ductility.
